additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 30: Records of processing activities
additions.quote: Each controller and, where applicable, the controller's representative, shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility.
additions.why: The nearest binding UK duty to a register: an organisation must keep a written record of its processing of personal data, with purposes, categories of data and recipients, and show it to the regulator on request. An AI system that handles personal data should already appear there. It covers personal data processing, not AI systems as such, and Art. 30(5) exempts organisations with fewer than 250 staff unless the processing is risky, not occasional, or involves special category data. Revised text as shown on the day read.

additions.title: Data protection audit framework, Accountability toolkit: Records of processing and lawful basis
additions.locator: Second control measure (record of processing activities), with its 'Ways to meet our expectations'; first control measure on data mapping
additions.quote: There is a formal, documented, comprehensive and accurate record of all processing activities (ROPA) based on a data mapping exercise that is reviewed regularly.
additions.why: How the regulator audits a record of this kind: built from a mapping exercise, not from memory; kept electronically; reviewed against what people actually do; with named responsibility for keeping it current. The same tests separate a live AI register from a snapshot. Carries the 'under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; the page shows no publication date, so the year is the year read. Data protection only, not AI governance in general.

additions.title: ETSI EN 304 223 V2.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
additions.locator: Clause 5.2.1, Principle 5 (Identify, track and protect the assets), Provisions 5.2.1-1 and 5.2.1-2, p.12
additions.quote: shall have processes and tools to track, authenticate, manage version control and secure their assets
additions.why: The free European Standard, adopted 8 December 2025, that carries the asset-inventory requirement of the UK's voluntary code into a formal standard (its history table shows it began as ETSI TS 104 223 in April 2025). It requires a comprehensive inventory of AI assets and the means to track them. A cyber security standard: 'assets' means models, data and related components, which is narrower than a register of AI uses with owner and risk tier. Voluntary unless adopted by contract or regulation.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, NIST AI 600-1
additions.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
additions.locator: Suggested actions GV-1.6-001 to GV-1.6-003 (under GOVERN 1.6), printed p.16 (PDF p.20)
additions.quote: Enumerate organizational GAI systems for incorporation into AI system inventory and adjust AI system inventory requirements to account for GAI risks.
additions.why: A free standard, dated 2024, that extends the framework's inventory outcome to generative AI. Its next action tells organisations to decide in policy how generative AI built into other software is treated in the inventory, which is the 'embedded systems' part of this criterion. Voluntary, US, and limited to generative AI.

additions.title: M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust
additions.publisher: Executive Office of the President, Office of Management and Budget (United States)
additions.locator: Appendix, section 3(b)(v) 'Update AI Use Case Inventories', PDF p.12; Chief AI Officer duty to maintain the inventory, PDF p.11
additions.quote: Each agency (except for the Department of Defense and the Intelligence Community) must inventory its AI use cases at least annually
additions.why: International comparator: US federal agencies must list their AI use cases at least once a year, send the list to the budget office and publish a version, with a named Chief AI Officer responsible for keeping it. A firmer and more regular duty than the UK's publication standard. A binding instruction to US federal agencies only, not law for businesses, and non-UK. The PDF is a scanned copy with machine-read text.

additions.title: Operationalising AI governance through ethics-based auditing: An industry case study
additions.publisher: Jakob Mökander and Luciano Floridi (arXiv; published in AI and Ethics)
additions.locator: Section 6.2 (Demarcating the material scope for AI governance), PDF p.14-15
additions.quote: Without such an inventory, AI auditors depended on the business to identify and select relevant projects and systems for the in-depth audits.
additions.why: A twelve-month case study of an AI audit at AstraZeneca. Without an agreed definition of what counted as AI the company could not assemble an inventory of its systems, so the auditors had to rely on the business to nominate what was examined. Direct evidence of what an incomplete register costs. Authors' arXiv preprint (posted 7 July 2024) of an article published in AI and Ethics in 2022 (doi 10.1007/s43681-022-00171-7); the journal copy could not be read. One company, one audit.

additions.title: Dutch Comfort: The limits of AI governance through municipal registers
additions.locator: Section on the registers' information voids, PDF p.10; see also p.4-5 and p.9
additions.quote: the algorithmic register only reveals those systems that are housed by the municipality
additions.why: A critical commentary on the public AI registers of Amsterdam and Helsinki: they listed a limited number of systems, left out the most harmful uses in welfare and policing, and missed systems run in the city by other bodies or third parties. A warning that a register can look complete and not be. Preprint as read (the arXiv page gives no journal reference); a commentary drawing on the authors' fieldwork, not a systematic study; about public registers in two cities, non-UK.

rejected.title: House of Commons Public Accounts Committee, Use of AI in Government (2025)
rejected.reason: Blocked: HTTP 403 with a 'Just a moment...' challenge page on committees.parliament.uk (publications.parliament.uk was already recorded as blocked in the domain log). Not bypassed, not cited.

rejected.title: Springer journal copies (AI & Society, Philosophy & Technology, AI and Ethics, Minds and Machines)
rejected.reason: Blocked: link.springer.com returned a 'Client Challenge' page to every request (four articles tried). Not bypassed. Where the author's own arXiv copy exists it was read instead; Novelli, Taddeo and Floridi on accountability, Santoni de Sio and Mecacci on responsibility gaps, and Mantymaki et al. on defining organisational AI governance were not read and are not cited.

rejected.title: NCSC and partners, Guidelines for secure AI system development (2023)
rejected.reason: Read ('Identify, track and protect your assets', PDF p.12). Not used: it makes the same asset-tracking point as the UK code already on this list and the ETSI standard added here, without requiring an inventory in terms.

rejected.title: ISO/IEC 42001
rejected.reason: Not retried: recorded as HTTP 403 in the domain log on 2 October 2026. No claim is made about it.

brief_check: Nothing contradicts the brief. Two points it does not mention: UK GDPR Article 30 already obliges most larger organisations to keep a record of personal data processing, an adjacent binding duty to 'No UK law requires an AI register by name'; and the asset-inventory provision of the government's voluntary AI cyber security code is now also in a European Standard, ETSI EN 304 223 V2.1.1 (adopted 8 December 2025).
